﴿When the sky is split asunder﴾ — infatarat: split open (inshaqqat); fujjirat: some of them were opened into one another, so that the sweet water mixed with the salt, the barrier (al-barzakh) between them disappeared, and the seas became one sea.

It is related that the earth will drink up the water after the seas have filled, so that it becomes level. This is the meaning of al-tasjir according to al-Hasan. It is also read fujjirat (with a light, unstressed doubling). Mujahid read fujjirat, with the verb in the active voice and with light pronunciation, meaning: they rebelled (baghat), because the barrier disappeared, in view of His words, ﴿They do not transgress (la yabghiyan)﴾, since al-baghy (rebellion) and al-fujur (wickedness) are brothers.

Ba'thara and bahthara have the same meaning, and both are composed of al-ba'th (raising) and al-bahth (searching), with an added raa' (r) that is pronounced with a damma. The meaning is: the graves will be overturned and their dead will be brought out. It has also been said that it refers to Surat al-Bara'a (al-Tawba), which is called al-Mubaʿthara, because it exposed (ba'thara) the secrets of the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 82, verses 6–8:

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?﴾, and how does the attribute of generosity fit with the denial of being deceived by Him? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?﴾, and how does the attribute of generosity fit ... etc.?"

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Zamakhshari's argument here is empty. The verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers, as is shown by His saying ﴿Nay, but you deny the Recompense﴾. We agree with him that they are eternal in the Fire and that their excuses are cut off, but not on the basis that their eternal punishment is obligatory upon God by the requirement of wisdom, for nothing is obligatory upon God. It is rationally permissible for Him to reward a disbeliever and place him eternally in Paradise, and the reverse for a believer. Were it not for the revealed texts affirming the reward of the believers and the punishment of the disbelievers, which make that conclusion necessary, what we have mentioned would remain a matter of possibility and conjecture, for God, Mighty and Majestic, does what He wills and decrees what He desires.]] A person is deceived only by one who is generous, as is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): he shouted at a servant of his, calling him several times, but the servant did not answer. He looked and found him at the door, and said to him: "Why did you not answer me?" He said: "Because I trust your forbearance and feel safe from your punishment." Ali admired his answer and freed him. They also said: "A man's generosity is shown by the bad manners of his servants."

I say: The meaning is that it is the duty of a human being not to be deceived by God's generosity toward him, in that He created him alive so that he might benefit, and by His bounty to him in this, so that, after He had empowered and obligated him and he disobeyed and denied the blessing bestowed upon him, he would hope that He would bestow upon him reward and remove punishment, out of deception by the first bounty. Such a thought is a denial and goes beyond the bounds of wisdom. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited it, said: "His ignorance deceived him." [[Abu 'Ubayd related it in Fada'il al-Qur'an from Kathir ibn Hisham, from Ja'far ibn Burqan, from Salih ibn Sammar, who said: "It reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and mentioned the same."]] Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "His foolishness and ignorance deceived him."

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, his wicked Satan deceived him, that is, he made sins attractive to him and said to him: 'Do whatever you wish, for your Lord is the Most Generous, who bestowed upon you what He bestowed at first, and He will bestow upon you at the end,' until he plunged him into ruin." It was said to al-Fudayl ibn Iyad: "If God raises you on the Day of Resurrection and says to you, 'What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?', what will you say?" He said: "I will say: 'Your veils, which were let down, deceived me.'" This is a confession of error in being deceived by the covering, not an excuse, as the one who desires greedily may think. The storytellers of the Hashwiyya (a term for a group of unlearned traditionalists, here used for the popular preachers) think of this and narrate from their imams that He said "concerning your Lord, the Most Generous" rather than any of His other attributes, so that His servant would be taught the answer, and say: "The generosity of the Generous deceived me."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: ﴿ma aghharak﴾ ("What has made you deceived?"), either as an exclamation of wonder or as a question, from your saying: "gharra al-rajul fa-huwa gharr," meaning he became heedless, as in your saying: "The enemy raided them while they were heedless (gharrun)." And "aghharahu ghayruhu" means another made him heedless.

﴿who created you, then proportioned you, then balanced you﴾: He made you whole, sound in limbs; ﴿then balanced you﴾: He made you upright and of proportionate form, without any disparity in it, so that He did not make one hand longer, nor one eye wider, nor some limbs white and others black, nor some hair dark and other hair blond. Or He made you of balanced form, walking upright, unlike the beasts. It is also recited ﴿fa-'adalak﴾ with the lighter form. There are two possible meanings. The first is that it has the sense of the intensive form: He balanced some of your limbs with others until you became balanced. The second is ﴿fa-sarrafak﴾ ("and He turned you"), as one says "'adalahu 'an al-tariq" (he turned him from the road): meaning He turned you away from the form of others and gave you a beautiful form distinct from all creation, or turned you toward some of the shapes and forms. The phrase ﴿ma shaa'﴾ ("whatever He willed") is an extra element, meaning: He fashioned you in whatever form His will and wisdom required from the forms that vary in beauty and ugliness, height and shortness, maleness and femaleness, resemblance to some relatives, and difference from resemblance.

If you ask: why was this clause not joined by a conjunction as the preceding clause was? I say: because it is an explanation of ﴿balanced you﴾. If you ask: with what does the prepositional phrase ﴿fi ayyi surah﴾ ("in whatever form") connect? I say: it may connect with ﴿rakkabak﴾ ("He assembled you"), in the sense: He placed you in some form and empowered you in it; or with an implied verb, meaning: He assembled you as existing in some form, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause if it is connected to an implied verb. It may also connect with ﴿fa-'adalak﴾, with ﴿ayy﴾ carrying the sense of wonder, meaning: so He balanced you in a wondrous form. Then He said ﴿ma shaa'a rakkabak﴾, meaning: He assembled you with whatever assemblies He willed, that is, an assembly that is beautiful.]

Translation:

Nay, [ceasing] from being deluded by the generosity of God and presuming upon it, which requires gratitude and obedience, to the opposite of these, which is disbelief and disobedience. Then He said, ﴿Nay, you deny the Religion﴾, [meaning] absolutely, and it is the recompense.

Or [it means] the religion of Islam. So you do not affirm reward or punishment, and this is worse than the reprehensible greed [mentioned above]. ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾: a confirmation of what they deny, namely the recompense, meaning that you deny the recompense while the recording angels write down your deeds so that you may be recompensed for them. In praising the recording angels, there is an exaltation of the matter of recompense, and that it is among the great matters with God; and were it not so, the noble angels, the guardians and recorders, would not have been appointed to preserve what they are held to account for and recompensed for. In this there is warning, intimidation, and exposure of the disobedient [[his words "wa-tashwir al-'usat" meaning "embarrassment", as in the margin; and in al-Sihah, "al-shiwar" means the branch, from which it is said: "shawwara bihi", as if he had exposed his nakedness. (A)]] and kindness to the believers. It is related from al-Fudayl that whenever he recited it he would say: "How severe a verse it is for the heedless."

In this there is warning, intimidation, and exposure of the disobedient [[his words "wa-tashwir al-'usat" meaning "embarrassment", as in the margin; and in al-Sihah, "al-shiwar" means the branch, from which it is said: "shawwara bihi", as if he had exposed his nakedness. (A)]] and kindness to the believers. It is related from al-Fudayl that whenever he recited it he would say: "How severe a verse it is for the heedless."

Qur'an 82:13–16 is the passage being commented on here. Its verses read:

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in pleasure. And indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.﴾ (13–14, not quoted in this excerpt)

The commentary reads:

"And they will not be absent from it" (وَما هُمْ عَنْها بِغائِبِينَ) is like His saying ﴿and they will not be removed from it﴾ (وَما هُمْ بِخارِجِينَ مِنْها) [Qur'an 2:167 / 5:37].

It is also permissible that the meaning is: they will burn in the Fire on the Day of Judgment, and they will not be absent from it before that, meaning: in their graves.

And it has been said: Allah informed in this surah that the son of Adam has three states: the state of life, in which his deeds are recorded; the state of the Hereafter, in which he is recompensed; and the state of the barzakh (intermediate realm), which is His saying ﴿and they will not be absent from it﴾ (وَما هُمْ عَنْها بِغائِبِينَ).

This means that the matter of the Day of Judgement is such that one cannot truly grasp its reality in terms of its terror and severity. However you imagine it, it is beyond that and many times greater. The repetition is for the sake of intensifying the awe. Then he summarised its description, saying: ﴿The Day when no soul will have power to do anything for another soul, and the command that Day will be entirely Allah's﴾. That is, no soul will be able to repel anything from itself, nor to benefit it in any way, and the command will belong to Allah alone.

Whoever reads ﴿يَوْمُ﴾ with a *damma* makes it an apposition (*badal*, a substitute noun that restates the preceding word) for ﴿يوم الدين﴾, or the meaning is: "It is a Day on which no soul will have power." Whoever reads it with a *fatha* does so by supposing an implied verb *yudānūn* (they will be held to account), since the word *al-Din* points to it, or by supposing an implied *udhkur* (remember). It is also permissible to read it with a *fatha* because it is attached to a non-declinable word (*ghayr mutamakkin*, a noun that does not take the full range of case endings) while it occupies a position in the nominative case.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites *Idhā al-samā'u infaṭarat* (Surah al-Infitar), Allah will record for him a good deed for every drop of rain from the sky, and a good deed for every grave."

[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
